title: Performance Under Time Pressure
tagline: Year 4 — Pacing tables, checkpoints, recovery from a bad stretch and the effect of rushing on accuracy

introduction.overview: Time pressure changes behaviour: people rush, skip checks and make more errors. The best defence is a plan made before the test: a pacing table with checkpoints, a rule for leaving stuck questions, and a short reset routine for when you notice panic. With these in place, a bad five minutes does not become a bad section. This chapter works through the arithmetic of pacing and the logic of recovery.
introduction.placementRelevance: Timed sectional tests make pacing and composure decisive.
introduction.realWorldContext: Working to deadlines uses the same plans and recovery habits.

learningObjectives: Build a pacing table with checkpoints
Compute time per question after a slow start
Estimate the score impact of rushing

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Required pace = time left ÷ questions left.

coreDefinitions: Pacing table: planned progress at set times.
Checkpoint: a time at which you compare progress with the table.
Reset: a deliberate pause to regain focus.
Recovery: returning to plan after a slow stretch.
Rush penalty: accuracy lost by hurrying.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Pressure is felt when you do not know where you stand; a table tells you.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: At each checkpoint compute required pace; if behind, skip harder questions rather than rushing all.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Checkpoint
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Done by t = t ÷ planned pace

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Catch-up
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Skip q questions to regain pace

mainNarrative: Plan: 30 questions in 45 minutes (90 s each). Checkpoints: after 15 minutes, 10 questions; after 30 minutes, 20 questions.
If after 15 minutes only 8 are done, 30 minutes remain for 22 questions: 82 seconds each, below plan. Skip two of the hardest to return to a 90-second pace.
If you rush all remaining questions and lose 10% accuracy, you give up about 2 correct answers out of 20.
A reset routine: stop, take one slow breath, re-read the stem, then go on; it takes ten seconds.
Leave stuck questions at about twice the average time.

deepDiveAspects.title: Front-loading
deepDiveAspects.content: It is better to be slightly ahead of plan early; late catch-up is harder.
